title: You Can Edit a TikTok in an Hour. Writing the First Line Can Take All Night.
markdown:
# You Can Edit a TikTok in an Hour. Writing the First Line Can Take All Night.

At 10:43 p.m., the footage is already on the timeline. The lighting is fine. The cuts are fast. You know how to make the video look like a TikTok. Then you open a blank notes app to write the voiceover, type "Hey guys," delete it, and stare at the cursor until the energy you had while filming has gone somewhere else.

That stall is common because writing and making are different jobs. Editing gives you material to react to: a face, a jump cut, a sound, a product in your hand. A blank script asks you to choose the point, the opening, the order, and the final line at once. The problem is rarely a lack of ideas. It is too many small decisions arriving before the first sentence.

You do not need a more elaborate content calendar to get past it. You need a repeatable way to turn one idea into words you can say out loud.

## Start with the moment that changed your mind

"I want to make a video about meal prep" is a topic, not yet a script. It leaves you with every possible angle: money, health, routines, recipes, containers, before-and-after shots. Pick the moment that made the topic worth filming.

Maybe it was opening the fridge on Wednesday and realizing lunch was already handled. Maybe it was the first time a recipe survived a busy week. Maybe it was the annoying mistake you made with soggy vegetables.

Write that moment as one plain sentence:

> I stopped buying lunch because I made the same two-hour mistake every Sunday.

That sentence gives the video a direction. It has a person, a change, and a little tension. You can film the fridge, the containers, the shopping bag, or the failed version. More importantly, you now know what the viewer is waiting to hear.

## Write hooks as promises, not greetings

A greeting asks the viewer for patience. A hook gives them a reason to stay. Before you draft the rest, write three openings that each make a slightly different promise.

- "I was wasting money on lunch because I was meal-prepping the wrong part."
- "The Sunday habit that made weekday lunch boring, but easy."
- "If your meal prep dies by Wednesday, try this before you buy new containers."

Read them aloud. The best hook is usually the one you could say without changing your voice. It should fit the footage you actually have and lead naturally to the next shot. If the opener promises a dramatic revelation while the video only shows a normal routine, the script will feel strained before the edit begins.

## Give each shot one job

New creators often try to write a paragraph, then hunt for visuals. Work in the other direction. Put a rough time beside each beat and decide what the viewer sees while you say it.

For a 30-second video, the page can be this small:

| Time | Say | Show |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0-3 sec | "I was wasting money on lunch because I prepped the wrong thing." | Opening the fridge on a weekday |
| 3-10 sec | "I used to cook five different lunches. By Wednesday, I did not want any of them." | Old containers or a quick reenactment |
| 10-22 sec | "Now I prep one base, then change the sauce and topping." | Building two versions side by side |
| 22-30 sec | "It is less exciting on Sunday. It makes Wednesday much easier." | Finished lunch going into a bag |

The spoken line moves the thought forward. The image proves it or makes it easier to picture. When both do the same work, cut one. You are writing for a phone screen, not a school essay.

## Leave room for how people talk

Your first draft can be clumsy. That is useful. Read it once while standing up, phone in hand, as if you were about to record. Mark every phrase that makes you slow down or sound like you are presenting slides. Replace it with words you would use in a voice note.

"I implemented a simplified preparation system" becomes "I stopped cooking five separate lunches."

The second version gives the viewer a picture. It also gives you an edit point. You can show five containers, then the one base. Specific language makes filming easier because it tells you what belongs on screen.

## End with the next useful thought

The last line does not have to be a hard sell. It can close the loop or give the viewer a simple next step. In the meal-prep example, "Pick one base for next week and change the sauce" works because it turns the story into an action.

If you want people to comment, ask about a real choice in the video: "Would you rather prep variety or make weekday lunch automatic?" Avoid a question that you do not care about just because it sounds like engagement bait. Viewers can feel the difference.

## When the blank page is the bottleneck

Use a template when you need it, but do not mistake a template for a finished script. A good script still has to match your topic, your footage, and the way you speak.

TikTok Script Pro is built for that specific handoff. Give it the topic, the facts you can stand behind, and your preferred length or tone. It returns hook options, a spoken script, on-screen text, visual cues, pacing, a caption, and a filming or posting tip. The output is meant to be recorded, then adjusted when your own voice says it differently.

The blank page does not need a grand solution. It needs a first angle, a line you can say, and a shot that carries the next beat. Once those are on the page, you can get back to the part you already know how to do: make the video.
